title: Understanding the Luci Ellis Salary: Hourly to Annual Conversion with Casual Loading and Super
description: Learn how to calculate the luci ellis salary from an hourly rate, including casual loading, super on top, tax, and fortnightly pay. Based on Fair Work rates.
salarySummary: For an employee earning the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour working 38 hours per week, the annual salary is approximately $52,245 before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage applies to employees not covered by an award or enterprise agreement. Award rates are higher and specific to industries or occupations, set by the Fair Work Commission. Use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides to find the correct rate for your job.

Casual loading is an additional 25% on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for the lack of paid leave. It is not included in the base rate; you add it separately. For example, if the base rate is $26.44, casual loading adds $6.61, making the casual rate $33.05 per hour.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in the annual salary figure?
faqs.a: No, superannuation is paid on top of your salary. The super guarantee rate is 12% of ordinary earnings (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830). It is not part of your take-home pay but is an additional benefit provided by the employer.

## Converting Hourly to Annual: The Basics

The simplest way to convert an hourly rate to an annual salary is to multiply by the number of hours worked per week and then by 52 weeks. For a full-time employee, the standard week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Act. This is the assumption used throughout this article unless stated otherwise. The formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For example, if you earn $30 per hour, your annual gross pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This figure does not include superannuation, which is paid on top.

### The Luci Ellis Salary Example

To make this concrete, let's consider the **luci ellis salary**. Suppose Luci Ellis is a casual employee earning the National Minimum Wage. From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour. For a 38-hour week, her annual gross pay is:

$26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44 (rounded to $52,245)

But as a casual, she is entitled to a 25% casual loading on top of the base rate. This loading is not included in the base rate; it is added separately. So her casual hourly rate is $26.44 × 1.25 = $33.05. If she works 38 hours per week at the casual rate, her annual gross pay becomes $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80. However, note that the casual loading compensates for the lack of paid leave entitlements. The base rate of $26.44 is the minimum for permanent employees; casuals get the loading.

### Using Fair Work Pay Guides

To determine the correct hourly rate for a specific job, you must check the applicable award. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides pay guides for each award that list minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. As noted on the Fair Work Ombudsman website, "Pay guides have the minimum pay rates for full-time, part-time and casual employees in an award". If your business has an enterprise agreement, that agreement may set different rates but cannot be less than the award base rate.

If you are unsure which award applies, the Fair Work Ombudsman offers guidance on their "I'm not sure what to pay my employees" page. They recommend knowing the employee's employment type, duties, and qualifications.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employees are paid fortnightly. To calculate fortnightly gross pay, multiply the weekly pay by 2. For the National Minimum Wage permanent employee: weekly pay = $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.72. Fortnightly = $2,009.44. For a casual at $33.05 per hour: weekly = $1,255.90, fortnightly = $2,511.80.

### Superannuation on Top

Superannuation is an additional payment made by the employer into the employee's super fund. It is not deducted from the salary; it is paid on top. The super guarantee rate for 2026–27 is 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For the **luci ellis salary** example at the permanent National Minimum Wage ($52,245), the super contribution would be $52,245 × 0.12 = $6,269.40, making the total employment cost $58,514.40. For the casual rate ($65,307), super would be $7,836.84, total cost $73,143.64. However, note that casual loading is part of ordinary earnings, so super is calculated on the loaded rate.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

The Australian Taxation Office's 2026–27 resident tax rates apply: nil tax on the first $18,200, 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000, 30% on $45,001 to $135,000, 37% on $135,001 to $190,000, and 45% above $190,000. The Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. For the permanent NMW salary of $52,245, the tax would be approximately $5,092 (using the scale) plus Medicare $1,045, leaving take-home pay of about $46,108. For the casual salary of $65,307, tax is about $9,092, Medicare $1,306, take-home $54,909. These are estimates; actual tax may vary with deductions and offsets.

### Distinguishing Minimum Wage, Award Rates, and Casual Loading

It is crucial to understand the hierarchy. The National Minimum Wage is the floor for employees not covered by an award or agreement. Award rates are higher and set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries. Casual loading of 25% is applied on top of the base award or minimum wage rate. Super is always on top of gross earnings. The Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay and Conditions Tool can help calculate exact figures.

### Internal Resources

For more detailed calculations, refer to our [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for current rates, and our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) guide for how loading interacts with other entitlements. You can also use our [pay guides](/blog) to find award-specific rates.

### Conclusion

The **luci ellis salary** example illustrates the importance of understanding each component: base rate, casual loading, super on top, and tax. Always verify the applicable award or minimum wage, and remember that super is an additional cost to the employer, not part of the employee's take-home pay. Use the Fair Work Ombudsman's resources to ensure compliance.
